Any sufficiently flexible model can reproduce your data exactly. It can pass through
every point, explain every wobble, and report an almost perfect fit. It will also be
worthless, because it has learned the noise in your particular survey along with the
signal.

This is overfitting, and it is the central problem of machine learning. Everything in
this section, the bias–variance trade-off, regularisation and hyperparameter selection,
is a response to it.

The marine version of the problem is sharper than the textbook version. With
autocorrelated data, a model can look like it is generalising when it is really just
memorising the neighbourhood.

## Findings from this section

Four results from these pages are worth knowing before you read them:

- On the coastal survey, ranking five models by **training** error gave the exact reverse of
  ranking them by test error. A tree fitted to a training RMSE of zero scored worse on new
  stations than predicting the mean and using no predictors at all.
- Adding **539 columns of pure random noise** to 540 training stations produced a training
  R² of exactly 1.000, and a test RMSE of 185, against a response whose largest observed
  value is 40.
- Splitting the error properly shows that the **irreducible noise is more than double**
  everything a model could control. Most of what looks like model error in marine count data
  is not model error.
- Lasso's selected variables are **not a stable finding**. Over 100 resampled fits, real
  predictors survived 24.7% of the time and pure noise columns 17.9%.

::: {.callout-note}
This section deliberately cheats until its last page: every earlier page chooses its
complexity by looking at the test set, and says so each time.
[Hyperparameter selection](hyperparameter-selection.qmd) is where that is done honestly, and
[section 7](../07-validation/index.qmd) is where the resampling itself is made appropriate to
marine data, because a random split of repeat visits to 160 sites flatters every number in
this section.
:::

- [Underfitting versus overfitting](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/model_selection/plot_underfitting_overfitting.html), scikit-learn. Three polynomial fits to the same points, which is this section's argument in one figure.
